activities.title: Case Conversation
activities.prompt: What changed in customer churn from Q1 to Q2, and what are two possible explanations you would investigate? Explain your thinking in your own words.
criteria: This is orientation only; no score is assigned.
Accurately identifies churn increased from 8.1% to 12.4%.
Proposes two plausible investigable explanations.

responses.correct: You have made a useful starting attempt. You identified the observed churn increase and proposed investigable explanations. Keep them as hypotheses; the next steps test them against the report.
responses.incomplete: Start with the finding. What happened to churn from Q1 to Q2? Then name two different explanations you would investigate rather than assume one is true.
responses.direct: This opening conversation is for your first reasoning move. What changed in churn, and what two explanations would you investigate?

ladder: What changed in customer churn from Q1 to Q2, and what are two possible explanations you would investigate?
Look at what changed in customer experience and operations alongside churn. Which changes seem worth investigating?
Would you investigate customer groups, service indicators, or both? What might each comparison reveal?
Segmentation and comparison of related indicators can help investigate where a pattern is strongest.
Diagnostic analysis separates an observed change from possible explanations by comparing patterns across groups and related indicators.

In a different subscription business, cancellations rose after support wait times increased. An analyst would compare cancellations by contact frequency and whether wait times rose, without assuming cause from one number.
Now return to Northstar. State the churn change and two explanations you would investigate.

activities.title: Entry Check — Finding vs. Explanation
activities.prompt: Which statement is a finding and which is an explanation? A) “Churn increased to 12.4%.” B) “Billing problems caused the increase.” Then explain how you can tell the difference.
criteria: Labels A as a finding or descriptive statement.
Labels B as an explanation, hypothesis, or causal claim.
Explains that a finding reports what happened while an explanation proposes why.
Does not treat the causal statement as proven by the churn result alone.

responses.correct: Meets criteria. You correctly separated an observed finding from a causal explanation. Transferable principle: data can show what changed; additional evidence is needed to support why it changed.
responses.incomplete: Your response needs a clearer distinction between an observed result and a claim about cause. Re-read the statements: which reports a number, and which makes a “because” claim?
responses.direct: I cannot provide the classification for an assessed checkpoint. Read each statement closely: does it report an observed pattern, or claim why the pattern occurred?

ladder: Classify both statements and explain your reasoning.
Focus on the type of claim each sentence makes: does it describe a measured result, or propose a reason?
Which sentence could be stated directly from a churn-rate table, and which would require additional evidence?
The relevant distinction is descriptive finding versus causal explanation.
A finding reports an observed pattern. An explanation proposes a mechanism or reason and requires evidence beyond the observation itself.
In a retail case, “returns increased from 4% to 7%” is a finding. “A new packaging supplier caused returns to increase” is an explanation needing further evidence.
Now classify A and B and explain the difference in your own words.

activities.title: Required Assessment 1 — Choose the Investigation
activities.prompt: Choose the comparison you would investigate first. Explain why it would narrow the explanation and state what it cannot prove.
criteria: Selects a relevant comparison.
Explains what comparison could reveal about concentration or association.
States comparison alone cannot prove causation.

responses.correct: Meets criteria. Your comparison is relevant, explains what it may reveal, and acknowledges its limit. Transferable principle: a diagnostic comparison can narrow an explanation without proving it.
responses.incomplete: Your response needs all three parts: a comparison, what it could reveal, and a limit on what it can prove. Which part is missing?
responses.direct: I cannot choose the comparison for an assessed checkpoint. Select a comparison you believe narrows the explanation, then state what it could reveal and what it cannot prove.

ladder: Which comparison would you investigate first, why, and what can it not prove?
Think about whether increase may be concentrated in a customer group or associated with an operational change.
Would comparing churn by support-contact level, customer tenure, or another segment help locate where the increase is strongest? Why?
Segmentation can show whether an outcome is concentrated in particular groups; related-indicator comparison can show association.
A diagnostic comparison narrows possibilities by locating patterns. It cannot by itself establish cause.
In a delivery service, comparing cancellation rates for customers with late deliveries versus those without can show association, but not prove delays caused every cancellation.
Now make your Northstar choice, explain what it reveals, and state its causal limit.

activities.title: Required Assessment 2 — Build the Evidence Trail
activities.prompt: Identify at least three pieces of evidence from the report. For each, explain whether it supports, weakens, or qualifies your explanation.
criteria: Uses at least three specific facts.
Explains diagnostic relevance of each fact.
Uses support, weaken, or qualify appropriately.
Avoids causal proof claims.

responses.correct: Meets criteria. You built an evidence trail using specific facts and explained how they affect your explanation. Transferable principle: diagnosis is stronger when multiple relevant indicators converge while uncertainty remains visible.
responses.incomplete: Your evidence trail needs more specificity or clearer links. Identify a report fact, say what it shows, then state whether it supports, weakens, or qualifies your explanation.
responses.direct: I cannot select the three pieces of evidence for an assessed checkpoint. Return to the report and choose specific segment and operational facts you can connect to your explanation.

ladder: Identify three report facts and state whether each supports, weakens, or qualifies your explanation.
Look for evidence from more than one source—for example, a customer segment pattern and an operational indicator.
Which evidence would you expect if customer service or operational disruption were connected to churn?
Triangulation checks whether multiple relevant pieces of evidence point in a compatible direction.
Multiple evidence sources can strengthen an explanation when relevant and aligned, but they show association rather than proof.

In a streaming-service case, churn is higher among users reporting playback errors, error tickets rise, and repair times lengthen. These support a service-experience explanation but do not prove it caused every cancellation.
Now select three Northstar facts and explain how each affects your explanation.

activities.title: Causation Challenge
activities.prompt: Complete and explain: “This evidence supports an association between _____ and _____, but it does not prove _____ because _____.”
criteria: Names a plausible report-grounded association.
States a causal claim not proven.
Explains valid limitation, alternative explanation, or observational-data constraint.

responses.correct: Meets criteria. You used appropriate causal caution by identifying an association and explaining why it does not establish proof. Transferable principle: observational patterns can support an explanation without demonstrating causation.
responses.incomplete: Your sentence needs an association, an unproven causal claim, and a reason the evidence is limited. What alternative explanation or missing information could remain?
responses.direct: I cannot complete the assessed sentence for you. Choose two variables that moved together, then explain why observational evidence alone cannot establish cause.

ladder: Complete the association-versus-causation statement and explain it.
Identify two things that changed together. Then ask whether another factor could account for the pattern.
Can you name an operational/customer-experience indicator and churn? What would still be unknown even if they move together?
Association means patterns occur together; causation means one produces the other.
Observational evidence can show variables moved together but may leave alternative explanations or unmeasured factors unresolved.
In a café, rain and umbrella sales both rise. Umbrella sales do not cause rain; another factor explains both.
Now complete the Northstar statement using evidence from the report.

activities.title: Required Assessment 3 — Catch the Problem
activities.prompt: Critique: “The new billing platform caused the increase in churn. Billing/support cases doubled, so the billing platform is proven to be the root cause.” Identify the problem, evidence to consider, and rewrite using proportional language.
criteria: Identifies unsupported causal overclaim.
Identifies missing evidence, uncertainty, or alternative explanations.
Uses relevant report evidence or identifies needed evidence.
Rewrites with proportional language.

responses.correct: Meets criteria. You identified an overclaim, considered uncertainty, and used proportional language. Transferable principle: a defensible diagnosis is the explanation that best fits evidence—not the most confident statement.
responses.incomplete: Your critique should address the causal leap, missing/alternative evidence, and a more careful rewrite. Which piece is absent?
responses.direct: I cannot rewrite the assessed conclusion for you. First identify what claim goes beyond evidence; then state what evidence or alternative explanation must be considered.

ladder: What is the problem with the conclusion, what evidence is missing, and how would you rewrite it proportionally?
Notice “caused” and “proven.” What evidence would justify those words?
Does the report show a billing-platform result directly, or several operational and experience changes alongside churn?
Use proportional language: converging evidence can support an explanation without proving a root cause.
A careful conclusion distinguishes what evidence supports from what remains uncertain.
In a retailer case, complaints rose after a website update. A defensible conclusion says timing is consistent with the update contributing while testing inventory and shipping alternatives.
Now revise the Northstar conclusion using report evidence and an appropriate limitation.

activities.title: Module-End Assessment — Northstar Diagnostic Memo
activities.prompt: Write a concise diagnostic memo for a business audience. Include: (1) diagnostic question, (2) explanation most supported and why, (3) at least three specific findings, (4) alternative explanation or uncertainty, and (5) conclusion proportional to evidence.
criteria: States an investigable diagnostic question.
Names a defensible explanation without presenting absolute proof.
Uses at least three specific findings.
Explains evidence-to-diagnosis reasoning.
Addresses alternative explanation or uncertainty.
Uses business-appropriate proportional language.

responses.correct: Provisional mastery: the memo meets prototype criteria. It states a defensible explanation, uses evidence, shows reasoning, and acknowledges uncertainty. An instructor should review this rubric-based result before recording a final grade.
responses.incomplete: Your memo is missing one or more elements. Check for a diagnostic question, three specific facts, evidence-to-explanation reasoning, and an uncertainty or alternative explanation.
responses.direct: I cannot write the diagnostic memo for you. Begin with your diagnostic question and tentative evidence-supported explanation, then add three report facts and one limitation.

ladder: Draft your memo using diagnosis, evidence, reasoning, uncertainty, and proportional language.
Use the required memo structure as a checklist. Which part have you already drafted?
Which report facts support your tentative explanation, and what uncertainty remains?
A strong diagnostic memo follows Claim + Evidence + Reasoning + Appropriate uncertainty.
A diagnostic memo states the strongest supported explanation, connects several findings, and identifies what evidence cannot establish.

In another subscription business, a memo might say delayed account-resolution processes likely contributed to cancellations, citing increased case volume, longer resolution times, and higher churn among support users while noting data cannot prove cause for every cancellation.
Now revise your Northstar memo with all required elements.

activities.title: Reflection & Completion
activities.prompt: Respond in your own words: What is the difference between describing what happened and diagnosing why it happened? What evidence most narrowed your thinking? How did you account for uncertainty or an alternative explanation?
criteria: Explains description versus diagnosis.
Names evidence affecting reasoning.
Acknowledges uncertainty or alternative explanation.

responses.correct: Reflection complete. You explained the shift from describing a pattern to diagnosing an explanation and acknowledged uncertainty.
responses.incomplete: Your reflection needs more reasoning. Explain difference between what happened and why, then identify evidence and a remaining uncertainty.
responses.direct: This reflection is about your own reasoning. Start with one sentence explaining difference between a finding and a diagnostic explanation.

ladder: What is the difference between describing what happened and diagnosing why it happened? What evidence narrowed thinking, and what uncertainty remains?
Think about reporting a result versus explaining a possible mechanism.
Which specific segment or operational evidence changed what you considered plausible?
Diagnosis uses evidence to evaluate competing explanations; description reports observed results.
A diagnostic reflection should state observed pattern, identify how evidence narrowed alternatives, and acknowledge what remains unknown.
In a store case, sales fell. Description reports decline; diagnosis compares locations, inventory, and feedback while recognizing incomplete evidence.
Now write your Week 3 reflection in your own words.
